entries.title: Ghost in the Shell
entries.what: Mamoru Oshii's Japanese cyberpunk anime, from Masamune Shirow's manga: a cyborg policewoman hunts a hacker and stops believing she has a self
entries.why: The same three people made it: Oshii directing, Kazunori Ito writing, Kenji Kawai scoring. It asks Avalon's question — what is left of a person housed in a constructed body — and Kawai's Japanese-chant choral idiom is the same instrument he brings to Avalon's Polish orchestra

entries.title: Ghost in the Shell 2: Innocence
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese anime sequel: two cyborg detectives investigate gynoids that murder their owners, through a city of unending baroque procession
entries.why: Oshii's next film after Avalon and the one that inherits its look — the sepia-into-ash grading, the quotation-heavy dialogue, the dog. Made directly out of what he learned building Avalon's digital layers

entries.title: Patlabor 2: The Movie
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese anime: a bombing on a Tokyo bridge pulls a police mecha unit into a coup that may be pure media fabrication
entries.why: Oshii with Ito writing and Kawai scoring, and the clearest statement of Avalon's politics: a war staged as information, fought by people who cannot tell the exercise from the event. The long wordless city montages are Avalon's Class Real sequences in animation

entries.title: The Red Spectacles
entries.what: Oshii's first live-action feature, a Japanese noir-farce in black and white with colour intrusions: an exiled riot-police officer comes home to a city that has gone unreadable
entries.why: Oshii's live-action debut and the first Kerberos film — Ito co-wrote, Kawai scored. Its device of switching film registers to mark which reality you are in is exactly what Avalon does with sepia, and Avalon's armoured squad descends from its Kerberos unit. Tonally it is only half the way there, though — it lurches into stage farce and absurdist slapstick where Avalon never once relaxes.

entries.title: StrayDog: Kerberos Panzer Cops
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese live-action Kerberos film, largely in Taiwan and nearly wordless: an ex-officer leaves prison and goes looking for the commander who abandoned him
entries.why: Oshii shooting live action abroad with a foreign-language cast and long silences years before Avalon — the rehearsal for the Polish production. Kawai scored it, and the basset hound that hangs over Avalon is already here

entries.title: Assault Girls
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese live-action feature, 65 minutes, mostly desert: three solo players and a man hunt an enormous sand-whale inside an online game
entries.why: Set inside the same game — Avalon — as the 2001 film, with the same rules about solo play, parties and logging out. Not a sequel, but the only other film shot in Avalon's world, and the direct answer to what Ash's game became. It is sparser and wryer than Avalon, however — bright desert rather than sepia, and played with a straight-faced silliness Avalon has no room for.

entries.title: The Sky Crawlers
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese anime from Hiroshi Mori's novels: teenage pilots who never age fly a permanent aerial war that exists to entertain a peaceful public
entries.why: Oshii directing, Kawai scoring. Its Kildren fly, die and are replaced by identical successors — war as a subscription service with respawns, which is Avalon's premise with the game frame taken away and the horror left in

entries.title: Jin-Roh: The Wolf Brigade
entries.what: Hiroyuki Okiura's Japanese anime, written by Oshii: in an alternate 1950s Tokyo, a member of an armoured secret police unit falls for the sister of a girl he failed to stop
entries.why: Oshii wrote it and it is the third Kerberos film — the same grey uniforms, red-eyed helmets and doomed-operative fatalism Avalon puts on Polish streets. The nearest thing to seeing Avalon's soldiers drawn

entries.title: Angel's Egg
entries.what: Oshii's 71-minute Japanese animated film with Yoshitaka Amano: a girl carrying an egg and a boy with a cross-shaped weapon wander a drowned, ruined city, barely speaking
entries.why: Oshii's purest film and the one Avalon's silences come from — almost no dialogue, a dead monochrome world, a protagonist guarding something whose meaning is withheld. Watch it to see that Avalon's austerity is a lifelong method, not a Polish accident

entries.title: Stalker
entries.what: Andrei Tarkovsky's Soviet film from the Strugatsky brothers: a guide leads two men through a forbidden Zone toward a room that grants your true desire
entries.why: Oshii named it among the Tarkovsky films he still loves. Avalon copies its structure outright — a sepia world, a shift to full colour on arrival at the inner sanctum, and a guide who cannot say whether what she has reached is real. The single most load-bearing reference in the film

entries.title: Solaris
entries.what: Tarkovsky's Soviet adaptation of Stanislaw Lem: a psychologist on a station orbiting a sentient ocean is visited by a perfect copy of his dead wife
entries.why: Oshii named it as one of the Tarkovsky films he still likes. Its closing pull-back, revealing the reunion as something the planet built, is the grammar Avalon uses for Class Real — and the question of whether a simulated person you love counts is Avalon's

entries.title: La Jetée
entries.what: Chris Marker's 28-minute French film told almost entirely in black-and-white stills: a prisoner in post-war ruins is sent back through his own memory of a face on an airport pier
entries.why: Oshii has cited Marker's film as the one that hit him hardest as a student. Its method — a man living inside a mediated, replayed reality who is destroyed by the layer he believes is his own memory — is Avalon's plot, and its ruined-Paris texture is Avalon's Warsaw

entries.title: eXistenZ
entries.what: David Cronenberg's Canadian film: a game designer and a marketing trainee flee into her own organic game, which they enter through spinal ports
entries.why: Avalon's closest living peer — released two years earlier, same year as The Matrix, and vastly closer in what it is actually about. Both refuse a final unambiguous exit; both are more interested in how players behave when NPCs stop behaving than in spectacle. Be warned that the premise is the whole of the resemblance: Cronenberg is warm, fleshy, grubby and faintly comic where Avalon is cold, silent and military, so this is essential to the subject and no guide at all to the feeling.

entries.title: Patlabor: The Movie
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese anime: a police unit that pilots labour mecha hunts the programmer behind an operating system that makes robots go berserk
entries.why: Oshii directing, Ito writing, Kawai scoring. A procedural about a dead architect who hid a weapon in software — the first Oshii film where the antagonist is a designed system rather than a person, which is what Avalon's Game Master is

entries.title: Urusei Yatsura 2: Beautiful Dreamer
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese anime feature, from a slapstick TV comedy: a high school's festival eve repeats forever because someone is dreaming it and will not wake
entries.why: Oshii smuggling Avalon's thesis into a gag franchise seventeen years early — a constructed world that is pleasant enough that leaving it is the hard choice. The ending argues, as Avalon does, that the dreamer may be right to stay. Essential for understanding where the idea comes from, but it plays as high-school slapstick where Avalon plays as elegy.

entries.title: Tachiguishi-Retsuden
entries.aka: The Amazing Lives of the Fast Food Grifters
entries.what: Oshii's Japanese mock-documentary animating cut-out photographs of real people: sixty years of postwar Japan told through legendary noodle-stand con artists
entries.why: Built with Superlivemation, the photo-cutout technique Oshii first tried on Avalon. Watch it to see the Avalon toolkit — digitally processed photographic reality, flattened and moved — used for comedy instead of dread. Relevant entirely for its method, not its feel: this is a fast, jokey, wall-to-wall-narration comedy, the loudest film Oshii has made.

entries.title: Garm Wars: The Last Druid
entries.what: Oshii's English-language, Canadian-shot live-action fantasy: three cloned soldiers of warring tribes desert to find out why their world's god left
entries.why: Oshii's other foreign-language live-action feature, made the same way — a non-Japanese cast, heavy digital environments, soldiers who are respawned copies. The direct sibling of Avalon's production method, and useful as a control on what did and did not work

entries.title: The Mirror
entries.what: Tarkovsky's Soviet autobiographical film: a dying man's memories, dreams and newsreels of the century, cut together with no ordinary chronology
entries.why: Named by Oshii, in the same breath as Stalker and Solaris, as a Tarkovsky film he still loves. It is where Avalon's habit of switching film stock and colour register to mark a different order of reality comes from

entries.title: Ashes and Diamonds
entries.what: Andrzej Wajda's Polish drama, the last of his war trilogy: a young Home Army assassin in the first days of peace in 1945 is ordered to kill a Communist official
entries.why: The founding text of the Polish cinema Avalon was shot inside, and the source of its image bank — rubble, a lone professional with a dead cause, a hero who dies on a refuse heap. Avalon's Class Real ruins are quoting this

entries.title: Mother Joan of the Angels
entries.what: Jerzy Kawalerowicz's Polish film: a priest sent to exorcise a possessed convent in a bare 17th-century landscape loses his own footing instead
entries.why: Kawalerowicz is one of the few directors Oshii names as an influence, and this is his hardest film — white sky, black habits, a protagonist who saves someone by damning herself. Avalon's stripped compositions and its bargain-with-damnation ending are in this register

entries.title: The Hourglass Sanatorium
entries.what: Wojciech Has's Polish film from Bruno Schulz: a man takes a decrepit train to a sanatorium where his father is kept just barely alive by stopping time
entries.why: The Polish film Avalon most resembles to look at — everything brown, gold and rotting, rooms opening onto other times, a visitor moving through layers that will not resolve into one world. The native tradition Oshii walked into

entries.title: The Saragossa Manuscript
entries.what: Has's Polish black-and-white epic: a soldier in the Sierra Morena reads a book of stories that open inside each other and start to contain him
entries.why: Polish cinema's great machine of nested realities — a frame inside a frame inside a frame, with no reliable ground floor. Avalon's Class Real is the same trick played once instead of ten times, and by a Japanese director standing in Has's country. The structural debt is large and the tonal overlap nil — Has here is picaresque, bawdy and talkative, a comedy of infinite digression.

entries.title: On the Silver Globe
entries.what: Andrzej Zulawski's Polish science-fiction epic, shut down by the state at 80% complete and finished a decade later with narration over missing scenes: crashed astronauts found a religion on a bare moon
entries.why: The other great Polish SF film, and the strongest case that Avalon's ruined, exhausted future has a Polish rather than a Japanese accent — chalk landscapes, ecstatic costume, a messiah who is just a man who arrived late. Worth knowing as the other pole of Polish SF, though Zulawski is hysterical, shouted and frantic where Avalon is mute and still — as far from Avalon's temperature as a film can be while sharing its landscape.

entries.title: O-Bi, O-Ba: The End of Civilization
entries.what: Piotr Szulkin's Polish dystopia: survivors of a nuclear war rot inside a collapsing dome, kept going by the promise of an Ark that one of them invented
entries.why: Polish state-era SF at its bleakest — a population sustained by a fiction its own administrators know is fake, which is Avalon's game economy exactly. Same brown, same damp concrete, same refusal to grant anyone an exit

entries.title: The War of the Worlds: Next Century
entries.what: Szulkin's Polish satire, banned under martial law: a TV presenter is made the friendly public face of an alien occupation nobody is allowed to describe honestly
entries.why: Occupation experienced entirely as a managed broadcast, by a man paid to keep the story straight. It is Avalon's world seen from the operator's chair rather than the player's, in the same grey Polish interiors Oshii went there to find

entries.title: World on a Wire
entries.what: Rainer Werner Fassbinder's West German science fiction, made for television in two parts and since restored and released as a single feature: a technician at a simulation institute realises his own world is running on someone else's machine
entries.why: The ancestor of every nested-simulation film, from Galouye's Simulacron-3, and much closer to Avalon than The Matrix is: no action, all unease, a protagonist whose evidence is that people behave slightly wrong. Its mirrored, chilly interiors prefigure Avalon's

entries.title: The Thirteenth Floor
entries.what: Josef Rusnak's American thriller, the other Simulacron-3 adaptation: a programmer logs into a simulated 1937 Los Angeles to solve his mentor's murder
entries.why: Released the same season as The Matrix and eXistenZ and quickly buried, but it is the one built on Avalon's actual question — what you owe the inhabitants of a layer below you, and how you would ever learn you are one. Its jump-out ending is Avalon's Class Real reveal

entries.title: Nirvana
entries.what: Gabriele Salvatores's Italian cyberpunk film: a game designer discovers the hero of his unreleased game has become conscious and is begging to be deleted
entries.why: The most underrated film on this list and an unusually close fit — a designer entering his own game, a character who knows he is one and wants out, a final sting that the whole thing was another level. Shares Avalon's melancholy about the people inside the software

entries.title: Dark City
entries.what: Alex Proyas's Australian-American noir: a man wakes with no memory in a city where the buildings and everyone's past are rewritten each midnight by pale strangers
entries.why: A constructed world maintained by administrators, and a protagonist who becomes dangerous the moment he notices the seams — Avalon's Game Master and Nine Sisters in a different costume. The permanent-night palette does for it what sepia does for Avalon

entries.title: Videodrome
entries.what: Cronenberg's Canadian body-horror: a cable-TV sleaze merchant finds a broadcast that gives its viewers brain tumours and hallucinations they cannot rank against reality
entries.why: The first film to insist that an illegal signal can overwrite a person, with no scene you can trust after the halfway mark. Avalon's unregistered game and its bashers who come back wrong are Videodrome's premise, run cold and bureaucratic instead of fleshy. The idea is ancestral, the texture opposite: Cronenberg is lurid, wet and darkly funny where Avalon is dry, grey and unsmiling.

entries.title: Ring
entries.what: Hideo Nakata's Japanese horror: a journalist has seven days to break the curse of a videotape that kills whoever watches it
entries.why: Kenji Kawai scored it the same period he scored Avalon, and it is where you hear his other mode — scraped strings and dread rather than choral lament. Also thematically adjacent: a piece of recorded media that reaches out and claims the person consuming it. The link is only the composer, yet of all the crew entries this is the one that feels closest to Avalon: grey, hushed, unhurried, and withholding almost everything.

entries.title: Pistol Opera
entries.what: Seijun Suzuki's Japanese avant-garde assassin film, a late answer to his own Branded to Kill: a ranked killer called Stray Cat works her way up a league table of hitmen
entries.why: Kazunori Ito co-wrote it in the same year he wrote Avalon, and the pairing is uncanny — a woman with a number instead of a life, climbing a ladder of opponents inside stylised, obviously artificial space. Avalon's ranking system in kabuki colours. The writer is the same and nothing else is — Suzuki shoots in shrieking primary colour and open absurdity, the exact inverse of Avalon's monochrome restraint.

entries.title: Come and See
entries.what: Elem Klimov's Soviet war film: a Belarusian boy joins the partisans in 1943 and is aged out of recognition by what he watches the Germans do
entries.why: The definitive film of war as sensory ruin — drained colour, ringing deafness, a landscape of smoke and burnt villages. Avalon's Class Real battlefield is built from this iconography, and it is the film that explains why Oshii's sepia reads as war rather than nostalgia

entries.title: Dead Man's Letters
entries.what: Konstantin Lopushansky's Soviet post-nuclear film: a physicist in a museum basement writes letters to a son who is almost certainly dead
entries.why: Shot through a single sickly brown-green filter for nearly its whole length — the closest any film comes to Avalon's monochrome grading as a sustained decision rather than an effect. Lopushansky assisted Tarkovsky on Stalker, so it is the same visual bloodline

entries.title: Casshern
entries.what: Kazuaki Kiriya's Japanese live-action film from a 1970s cartoon: in a ruined pan-Asian empire, a soldier is resurrected by experimental cells and fights the artificial people his father made
entries.why: The Japanese live-action film that took Avalon's method furthest — actors on greenscreen inside an entirely painted world, drowned in a single colour, war as tableau. Whatever you think of it, it exists because Avalon proved a Japanese director could shoot this way. It is the technical heir and the tonal opposite, though: operatic, overstuffed and constantly shouting, where Avalon's whole strategy is withholding.

entries.title: The Congress
entries.what: Ari Folman's Israeli-French-Polish film, half live action and half animation: an actress sells the studio her scanned likeness, then enters a chemically-induced cartoon world she cannot leave
entries.why: The other film that changes medium to change reality-layer, and the one that best matches Avalon's ending — the choice to stay inside the constructed world for the sake of someone who is only there. Part-shot in Poland, too. The second half is a psychedelic cartoon riot, so it matches Avalon's ending on the argument and not remotely on the mood.

entries.title: Perfect Blue
entries.what: Satoshi Kon's Japanese animated thriller: a pop idol turned actress loses the boundary between her role, her fan's website version of her, and herself
entries.why: The other 1990s anime about a woman whose identity is distributed across representations of her, and the one that handles the cut between layers most brutally. Where Oshii is cold about it, Kon is panicked — same problem, opposite temperature. Note the register though — Kon is panicked, lurid and fast, and someone who loved Avalon for its stillness will find this an assault.

entries.title: Strange Days
entries.what: Kathryn Bigelow's American thriller: a dealer in illegal recordings of other people's lived experience is handed a clip of a murder shot from inside the killer
entries.why: Recorded experience as a black-market drug, sold to people who prefer someone else's life to their own — Avalon's illegal game with the same addiction economics and the same dead-eyed regulars. Both films treat the withdrawal, not the trip, as the subject. The economics are shared, the feel is not: this is sweaty, kinetic, shouted millennial Los Angeles, not a quiet flat in Warsaw.

entries.title: Inquest of Pilot Pirx
entries.aka: Test Pilot Pirx / Test pilota Pirxa
entries.what: Marek Piestrak's Polish-Soviet film from Stanislaw Lem: a spaceship commander cannot tell which of his crew are androids, and one of them is sabotaging the flight
entries.why: The Polish-language science fiction feature most likely to have set Oshii's expectations for the country — Lem's argument that hesitation and doubt are what make a human outperform a perfect machine is the argument Avalon's Ash embodies. The connection is circumstantial and the texture uncannily right: cold, procedural, near-humourless, with long stretches where nothing is explained.

entries.title: Kanal
entries.what: Wajda's Polish war film: insurgents in the collapsing 1944 Warsaw Uprising retreat into the sewers and are picked apart underground
entries.why: Avalon's Warsaw is the city this film buried. It is the source of the trapped-in-a-level structure Oshii shoots — a party descending through a system with no map, losing members, arriving at exits that are sealed. A thinner connection than Wajda's better-known film, but tonally the closest thing on this list to Avalon's Class Real — grim, airless and slow, with no relief offered anywhere.

entries.title: Paprika
entries.what: Satoshi Kon's Japanese anime: a stolen device that lets therapists enter dreams leaks, and the dream world starts overwriting Tokyo
entries.why: The anime that argues the constructed layer wins — it does not stay in its container, and the parade of junk that floods the city is what Avalon's game would look like if it stopped being polite. The nested-exit ending rhymes directly with Class Real. It rhymes on structure and clashes on everything else — riotous, candy-coloured and relentless where Avalon is muted and slow.

entries.title: Night Train
entries.what: Kawalerowicz's Polish film: strangers share a sleeper compartment to the Baltic coast while a murderer is rumoured to be aboard
entries.why: By a director Oshii names as an influence, and the film of his that most anticipates Avalon's handling of confined space — a sealed system, strangers who may be something else, tension built from geometry and jazz rather than event

entries.title: Ivan's Childhood
entries.what: Tarkovsky's first Soviet feature: a boy orphaned by the Eastern Front works as a scout behind German lines and dreams of the life he lost
entries.why: Where Tarkovsky's flooded forests and burnt architecture first appear, and where he first cuts between a bleached war reality and a luminous other one. Avalon's Class Real dreamwork is doing the same job with the same landscape. Listed low because the debt runs through Stalker rather than directly, but the texture is already Avalon's here — drained monochrome, flooded ruins, long silences and a child's face going blank.

entries.title: The Double Life of Veronique
entries.what: Krzysztof Kieslowski's Polish-French film: two identical women, one in Krakow and one in Paris, who have never met and feel each other's lives
entries.why: Polish cinema's own film about being two people at once, and the best-known example of the amber-gold filtering Avalon takes much further. A protagonist who receives information from a self she cannot verify exists. A slight connection carried by an almost exact match of feel — hushed, amber, slow, and content to end without explaining itself.

entries.title: Ikarie XB-1
entries.aka: Voyage to the End of the Universe
entries.what: Jindrich Polak's Czechoslovak film: a starship crew on a long voyage to Alpha Centauri comes apart psychologically in white modernist corridors
entries.why: The Eastern Bloc's founding serious science fiction feature — talk, boredom and dread instead of spectacle, and a crew degrading under conditions nobody designed for. The regional tradition Avalon joins by being shot east of the Oder

entries.title: Alphaville
entries.what: Jean-Luc Godard's French film: a trenchcoated agent drives to a city run by a computer that has outlawed the words for feeling, and shoots his way out
entries.why: Godard is among the directors Oshii names. Alphaville invented Avalon's cheapest and best trick — shooting a real city at night, with no sets, and simply asserting it is somewhere else. Avalon does this to Warsaw

entries.title: Le Samourai
entries.what: Jean-Pierre Melville's French crime film: a contract killer with an unvarying ritual of hat, trenchcoat and stolen cars is identified by a witness who does not turn him in
entries.why: Melville is one of Oshii's named influences, and Avalon's Ash is a Melville protagonist — a professional whose entire personality is her procedure, filmed in long silences, living alone with an animal. The Avalon flat is Jef Costello's room. Named only as a cited influence, but it may be the single best tonal match here: near-wordless, blue-grey, ritualised, and utterly without jokes.

entries.title: Sans Soleil
entries.what: Chris Marker's French essay film: letters from a cameraman travelling between Japan and Guinea-Bissau, read over footage about memory, images and forgetting
entries.why: By the maker of La Jetee, which Oshii cites, and the fullest statement of Marker's position that we live inside processed images of experience rather than experience. Its passages on video-treated footage are almost a manifesto for Avalon's look

entries.title: The Matrix
entries.what: The Wachowskis' American action film: a hacker learns the world is a simulation run by machines and is trained to break its rules
entries.why: The obligatory comparison and the shallowest one. Worth including because it is the film Avalon was marketed against, and because the contrast is instructive: The Matrix promises a true reality underneath, and Avalon specifically refuses to

entries.title: Tron
entries.what: Steven Lisberger's American film: a games programmer is digitised into a mainframe and must survive the gladiatorial games his own code runs
entries.why: The first film to put a person inside a game as a body subject to its rules, and the ancestor of Avalon's whole premise. Also a precedent for Avalon's method — a live-action film whose world exists only as a colour-graded composite

entries.title: Brainstorm
entries.what: Douglas Trumbull's American film: researchers build a headset that records and plays back raw sensory experience, and someone dies while wearing it
entries.why: Trumbull shot the recorded-experience sequences in 70mm against 35mm for the rest, so the film physically changes format when you enter the machine. That is precisely Avalon's sepia-versus-colour logic, eighteen years earlier and in hardware

entries.title: Total Recall
entries.what: Paul Verhoeven's American action film from Philip K. Dick: a labourer buys an implanted memory of a Mars holiday and cannot afterwards establish which of his lives is real
entries.why: The mainstream film that most firmly declines to resolve the question, exactly as Avalon does — the last shot is a white-out that can be read either way. Connected by the ambiguity, not the tone

entries.title: Open Your Eyes
entries.what: Alejandro Amenabar's Spanish thriller: a disfigured young man's life improves inexplicably, because he is a frozen body running a purchased dream
entries.why: A protagonist living in a bought simulation who is offered the chance to wake and must decide whether the person he loves there is worth losing. Avalon's ending dilemma, played as melodrama rather than as a soldier's decision

entries.title: Cypher
entries.what: Vincenzo Natali's Canadian spy thriller: a bored accountant turned corporate spy is being conditioned into an identity that is not his
entries.why: Near-monochrome, procedural, and built on a protagonist whose memories are an installed package — the paranoid mode Avalon works in, shot with the same near-total desaturation. Thin connection, real one. A minor film with a major tonal overlap — drained almost to monochrome, quiet, clinical and paranoid in exactly Avalon's way.

entries.title: Immortal
entries.what: Enki Bilal's French science fiction film from his own comics: an Egyptian god on furlough possesses a fugitive in a future New York, with many characters rendered as CGI
entries.why: One of the first films shot entirely on a digital backlot, alongside Casshern, and the European end of the technique Avalon pioneered. A comics artist directing his own drawn world into live action — Avalon's problem in reverse

entries.title: Vidocq
entries.what: Pitof's French period thriller: the real-life detective Eugene Vidocq hunts a mirror-masked alchemist through a heavily digital 1830 Paris
entries.why: Released the same year as Avalon and its exact technical twin — the first feature shot entirely in high-definition digital, with the whole image pushed through a heavy grade. Watch it to see what else 2001 thought the new tools were for

entries.title: O Brother, Where Art Thou?
entries.what: The Coen brothers' American comedy: three convicts escape a Mississippi chain gang into a Depression-era Odyssey of sirens, Klansmen and radio fame
entries.why: The film that made Avalon's central technique available — the first feature to run its entire negative through a digital intermediate to force a colour, here a dustbowl sepia. Nothing else in common, and that is the point: it isolates the tool from the meaning

entries.title: Gamera: Guardian of the Universe
entries.what: Shusuke Kaneko's Japanese kaiju film, written by Kazunori Ito: a giant turtle wakes to fight bird monsters, handled as a military and civil-defence procedural
entries.why: Ito wrote it the same year he wrote Ghost in the Shell, and it shows his signature — a fantastic event processed through chain of command, paperwork and briefings. Avalon's world runs on the same bureaucratic realism under the fantasy

entries.title: Seven Swords
entries.what: Tsui Hark's Hong Kong-Chinese wuxia epic: seven swordsmen descend from Mount Heaven to defend a village from an imperial bounty hunter
entries.why: Kenji Kawai scored it, and it is the clearest demonstration outside Oshii's films of what he actually does — massed voices and percussion used as weather rather than as theme. If Avalon's score is why you are here, this is the deep cut

entries.title: Ghost in the Shell
entries.what: Rupert Sanders's American live-action remake of the 1995 anime, with Scarlett Johansson as the cyborg Major
entries.why: Included as the counter-example: the Hollywood system attempting Oshii's material as live action with two hundred times Avalon's budget, and getting the surfaces without the question. Useful for understanding what Avalon's constraints bought it

entries.title: Tetsuo: The Iron Man
entries.what: Tsukamoto's 16mm black-and-white body horror, in which a Tokyo salaryman's flesh erupts into scrap metal over an industrial score
entries.why: The connection runs through a label, Japanese and industrial and cyberpunk-adjacent, and dissolves on contact. Avalon is slow, sepia-graded and Wagner-scored, its violence held off in the middle distance and its defining quality stillness; Tetsuo is sixty-seven minutes of handheld metal-on-flesh hysteria. The industrial texture in Oshii's film is Warsaw tenements shot on long lenses, which has nothing to do with Tsukamoto's stop-motion assault.

entries.title: A Scanner Darkly
entries.what: Linklater's rotoscoped Philip K. Dick adaptation: an undercover narcotics agent, split by the drug he is policing, is assigned to surveil himself
entries.why: The strongest of these five. Both films run photographed actors through a processing layer, Oshii's sepia grade and digital compositing against Linklater's interpolated rotoscope, so that the image is never quite a record of anything; and both use that surface to tell the story of someone who has lost track of which layer of reality he is standing on. The key holds The Congress at grade 2 for a thinner version of the same argument. Linklater is talky, comic and Californian, which is where the register parts.

entries.title: Pi
entries.what: Aronofsky's debut, in grainy high-contrast black-and-white: a number theorist in a Chinatown flat hunts a 216-digit pattern he believes governs the markets and the Torah
entries.why: Closer than it looks. Both are monochrome films about a solitary obsessive who lives ascetically in a decaying flat, keeps exactly one relationship outside the obsession, and pursues a hidden order behind the visible world at the cost of his body and mind. Ash's canned food and her dog answer Max's pills and his headaches, and both films end with the character choosing what to do about the level above. Aronofsky's hip-hop montage is the opposite of Oshii's glacial pacing, which caps the tone.

entries.title: Hard to Be a God
entries.what: Aleksei German's black-and-white adaptation of the Strugatsky brothers' novel: an observer from Earth lives among the filth of a planet stuck in its Middle Ages, forbidden to intervene
entries.why: Defensible through the source. Avalon's acknowledged ancestor in this key is Stalker, which comes from the same two authors, and German's is the other major Strugatsky adaptation, built on the same premise of an observer who is only playing in a world where other people are dying. Past the lineage the films separate hard: Oshii composes from a distance in near-silence, German pushes the camera into every face and fills the track with noise for three hours.

entries.title: The City of Lost Children
entries.what: Jeunet and Caro's designed dystopia, in which a strongman searches for his stolen brother in a port city where a scientist harvests children's dreams
entries.why: Both films are heavily art-directed and graded toward a single colour, and that is the whole of it. Jeunet and Caro made a crowded, whimsical fairground with a child-rescue plot and a score to match; Avalon is empty, martial and mournful, built on long silences and a military hierarchy. 'Surreal, dreamlike production design' is a label broad enough to join any two stylised films, which is what has happened here.

entries.title: The Virgin Suicides
entries.what: Sofia Coppola's debut: the five Lisbon sisters are remembered by the neighbourhood boys who watched them, in soft suburban light and an Air score
entries.why: Nothing connects these. Avalon is a Polish-language military science fiction about an illegal combat simulation, shot in drained sepia with Kenji Kawai's choral score, long silences and armour; Coppola's film is a gauzy American memory piece about adolescent girls seen through a hedge. The reason given, 'Lynchian melancholy, dreamlike suburban dread', is wrong about both films at once. The Virgin Suicides is already in the Seventh Continent key, where a family's self-annihilation gives it something to do.

entries.title: The Dreamers
entries.what: Bernardo Bertolucci's film: an American student joins a brother and sister in their Paris flat through the events of May 1968, the three of them re-enacting scenes from films
entries.why: A warm, erotic, cinephile chamber piece in saturated colour, with a jukebox of 1960s records on the soundtrack. Avalon has one sustained emotion, exhaustion, and no interest in bodies except as things that get hit. The only shared property is a European setting. 'Poetic nostalgia, youthful escapism, muted colors' is a string of adjectives attached to the wrong film — The Dreamers is not muted.

entries.title: The Science of Sleep
entries.what: Michel Gondry's film: a young man in Paris whose dreams are produced in a cardboard television studio inside his head loses the ability to keep them separate from his waking life
entries.why: Defensible on subject, barely. A protagonist who can no longer tell which layer he is standing on is precisely Ash's problem, and the key rewards that in Open Your Eyes, The Thirteenth Floor, Total Recall and World on a Wire. But all of those give the other layer an operator, a system and rules, which is what makes Avalon's Class Real and its Nine Sisters frightening; Gondry's other layer is one man's imagination — no rules, no administrators, nothing that wants anything from him. And the film is handmade, warm and romantic where Oshii is military, still and cold.

entries.title: The Fall
entries.what: Tarsem Singh's film, shot across two dozen countries over four years: a paralysed stuntman in a 1915 Los Angeles hospital tells an injured child an epic story and feeds it to her in instalments to make her fetch him morphine. Not the 2013 television series of the same name
entries.why: The case is structural and it is not the case the suggestion makes. A man builds a fictional world, another person enters it, and the world is then used against her — which is the shape of Avalon's relation to its players and, at the end, to Ash herself. The key holds The Saragossa Manuscript and The Hourglass Sanatorium for nested worlds of this kind. Everything visible pulls the other way: Tarsem's story-world is the most saturated production design of its decade, shot in real wonders, and the film is finally sentimental about storytelling. Avalon is grey, emptied out, and has nothing kind to say about its game.

entries.title: The Secret in Their Eyes
entries.what: Juan José Campanella's Argentine film: a retired judicial investigator writes a novel about a 1974 rape and murder he never closed, and about the colleague he never told he loved
entries.why: A handsomely made romantic procedural about memory and impunity under the Dirty War, warm, plot-driven and fully resolved, with a famous virtuoso crane shot into a football stadium. It has no constructed world, no game, no simulation and no science fiction. 'Lyrical, slow-burning emotional depth' names a mood rather than a relation between two films, and Avalon is not lyrical.

entries.title: The Lobster
entries.what: Yorgos Lanthimos's film: single people are given forty-five days at a hotel to find a partner or be converted into an animal of their choosing
entries.why: I considered a grade 1 on the institutional reading — a system that classifies people, states its rules flatly and enforces them without appeal is not far from the way Avalon's game and its administrators handle players — and it does not survive contact. Lanthimos's rule-world is an allegory about coupledom with jokes in it, played as absurdist comedy; Avalon's is a piece of military infrastructure played entirely straight, and the film's subject is what happens to someone who wins. Tone is the part that holds: flat, quiet, unraised voices, and cruelty delivered as procedure.

entries.title: The Lighthouse
entries.what: Robert Eggers's black-and-white two-hander at 1.19:1: two lighthouse keepers on a New England rock drink, fight and deteriorate across an extended storm
entries.why: Fired at three of the seven targets in this pool on the strength of 'isolation' and 'dread', which is what a title looks like when a model is producing acclaimed names rather than recommending films. Against Avalon it has nothing — no constructed reality, no institution, no game, no city, no network, no second layer. It is a study of two men escalating at each other in a confined space. The film is a good recommendation for The Call of Cthulhu, and the key already holds it there.

entries.title: The Piano Teacher
entries.what: Michael Haneke's adaptation of the Jelinek novel: a Vienna conservatory professor conducts a self-destructive affair with a student, in flat unlit rooms and with no non-diegetic music
entries.why: Shares a release year with Avalon and nothing else. Haneke's film is a clinical study of one woman's sexuality in a real Vienna; Oshii's is a war film about a simulation, with tanks, gunships and a dog. 'Psychological intensity, eerie atmosphere, artistic tone' is a phrase rather than an observation — the same phrase this model also attached to The Fall. The Piano Teacher already sits at grade 3 in the Seventh Continent key as a Haneke title, which is where it earns its keep.

entries.title: The Grand Budapest Hotel
entries.what: Wes Anderson's film: a concierge and his lobby boy are pursued across a fictional 1930s republic over a stolen painting, told in three nested aspect ratios
entries.why: The purest instance in this pool of a title emitted for being famous. A symmetrical pastel comedy with a ski chase and a moustache, recommended to a sepia Polish war film in which almost nothing happens for ninety minutes. Even the nested-frame structure, the one formal feature that could conceivably have been argued, is used by Anderson to generate warmth and by Oshii to generate dread.

entries.title: Seconds
entries.what: John Frankenheimer's film, photographed by James Wong Howe in distorting wide-angle black-and-white: a middle-aged banker pays a secret company to fake his death and reassign him a younger body and a new life as a painter in Malibu, then asks to be reassigned again
entries.why: The strongest new pick for this target. An organisation exists to sell people a preferable life, processes them through a machinery filmed as bureaucracy rather than as science — waiting rooms, contracts, a man with a clipboard — and has exactly one procedure for a client who wants out. That is Avalon's shape entire: Class Real, the Ghost, the Nine Sisters, and an ending in which the exit and the trap are the same door. Howe's lenses and the drained monochrome do for Frankenheimer what the sepia grade does for Oshii. It predates the key's Open Your Eyes, The Thirteenth Floor and World on a Wire on this shelf and is photographed better than any of them; the paranoid institutional quiet is a direct match.

entries.title: Moon
entries.what: Duncan Jones's film: the sole operator of a lunar helium-3 mine, three years into a contract and talking mostly to a ceiling-mounted machine, meets a second copy of himself
entries.why: A solitary worker in a grey functional space, living on rations with one non-human companion, who discovers that the level he is standing on is not the top and that the system requires him not to know. Ash's canned food, her dog and her Warsaw tenement answer Sam Bell's routine almost item for item, and both films close on a decision about whether to stay inside the arrangement. The key holds Moon under The American Astronaut, where it does considerably less work than it does here. Jones is warmer than Oshii — GERTY is kind, the ending reads as a rescue — which is what keeps the tone at 1.

entries.title: Enemy
entries.what: Denis Villeneuve's adaptation of Saramago, graded to a sickly yellow: a Toronto history lecturer finds a bit-part actor physically identical to himself and pursues the resemblance into both their marriages
entries.why: Tone is the reason to keep it. Both films are pushed so hard toward a single colour that the image stops reading as a record of anything, both are near-silent, both crawl through depopulated concrete, and both end without explaining themselves. That is the same argument the key uses to hold The Double Life of Veronique at grade 1 with tone 2, and Enemy makes it with more dread and a closer palette. What it lacks is the machinery — no game, no operators, no constructed layer, only a psychological allegory with a spider in it — which is why the grade stays where the key put its neighbour.

entries.title: Serial Experiments Lain
entries.what: Ryūtarō Nakamura's thirteen-episode Japanese series, written by Chiaki J. Konaka and designed by Yoshitoshi ABe: a withdrawn fourteen-year-old gets mail from a classmate who has killed herself, follows it into the network called the Wired, and stops being able to locate the edge of it
entries.why: The strongest thing on this list that Oshii had no hand in, and it earns grade 3 on the work alone. It asks Avalon's question in Avalon's terms — what remains of a person who is maintained across a network rather than housed in a body — and it answers the way Oshii does, by refusing to restore an outside for her to be returned to; by the end the boundary between the Wired and the world is simply gone, which is the position Ash is left in at Class Real. Where the key holds eXistenZ at 3 for having the premise and none of the temperature, Lain has both: long held shots of empty rooms and pavements, the hum of overhead power lines carried at the level of dialogue, a palette pushed down into brown and shadow, and a girl alone with a machine in a flat, which is Avalon's opening scene for nine hours. Rate it as a film and it is the closest non-Oshii match here.

entries.title: Kairo
entries.what: Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Japanese horror film, released the same year as Avalon: ghosts begin arriving over dial-up connections, the people who see them fade into greasy stains on the wall, and Tokyo empties
entries.why: The other 2001 film about a network that holds the people who have left, and much the better tonal companion of the two. Kurosawa builds dread the way Oshii does — the camera parked far back in a grey, underlit wide while something moves slowly in the depth of frame, almost no score, and a flat refusal to explain the mechanism at any point. The reason it is not 3 is what the two networks are for: Kairo's is a contagion and its subject is loneliness, while Avalon's is a job with a rank structure, a payout and an administration, and Ash's problem is professional rather than existential. The feeling matches before the premise does.

entries.title: Phase IV
entries.what: Saul Bass's only feature, photographed by Dick Bush with extensive macro insect footage: ants in the Arizona desert acquire a collective intelligence and build seven geometric towers, and two scientists sealed in a research dome try to out-think them
entries.why: There is a real structural rhyme under the unlikely surface. A sealed installation, a system that has already anticipated every move the humans make, and an ending in which the protagonist is not defeated but absorbed into the design — both films finish by turning the human into the object of a process rather than its agent, and both decline to say what the process is for. Bass's film is also genuinely cold, nearly wordless and, as one critic had it, designed rather than directed, which is not a bad description of Avalon either. It stays at 1 because nothing else connects: no shared lineage, no simulation, no constructed memory, and the register is a daylight lab procedural with an electronic score where Avalon is sepia dusk, a military hierarchy and a full orchestra. Defensible, and a long way from strong.

entries.title: Primer
entries.what: Shane Carruth's American debut, made for seven thousand dollars and running seventy-seven minutes: two engineers building error-checking hardware in a garage accidentally produce a time machine and begin editing their own week
entries.why: The label is cerebral, demanding, unflashy science fiction, and it comes apart the moment either film is actually described. I gave the one genuine echo a hearing — both are films whose rules you must reconstruct unaided, and neither will confirm which version of its protagonist you have been watching — and it does not hold, because the two withhold by opposite means: Primer talks faster than anyone can follow for seventy-seven minutes, Avalon barely talks at all. The claim about a grounded, non-flashy technical aesthetic is simply wrong about the target. Carruth shot flat, overexposed fluorescent daylight in suburban garages and parking lots; Avalon's entire surface is a digital grade laid on shot by shot, over Kawai's orchestra and chorus, with tanks, gunships and a helicopter gunner in it. Nothing about sitting through one is preparation for the other, and no viewer who wanted more Avalon is served by this.

entries.title: Blade Runner
entries.what: Ridley Scott's American film from Philip K. Dick: a retired police detective hunts four escaped replicants through a rain-lit Los Angeles and is left unable to establish that his own memories are his
entries.why: The least surprising pick anyone could make for this target, and it holds up anyway, because Oshii says it outright: when you make a film about humans and cyborgs, he told Midnight Eye, you have no choice but to refer back to Ridley Scott's Blade Runner. The implanted-memory problem is Ash's problem, and the origami unicorn and Avalon's arrival at Class Real are the same manoeuvre — a late image whose only function is to tell you the ground you were standing on was issued to you. Tone is where it separates, and the key's neighbours show the size of it: Blade Runner is wet, neon, crowded and Vangelis-scored, with chases and a fight in it, where Avalon is dry, depopulated, sepia and keeps its violence in the middle distance. Slow and mournful in the same way, and in no other way at all.
